t: A particle executes SHM with an angular frequency ω=4π rad/s. If it is at its extreme position initially, then find the instants when it is at a distance √3/2 times its amplitude, from the mean position.
s:
Let a be the amplitude and ϕ the phase constant for the oscillation.
The displacement equation can be written as
x=asin(4πt+ϕ) [∵ω=4π_(rad/s)]
Since at t=0; x=+a, therefore 4π(0)+ϕ=π/2⇒ϕ=π/2
∴ x=asin(4πt+π/2)=acos(4πt)
Now let tₙ be the instant when the particle’s displacement s
√3a/2,nth
Evidently ±√3a/2=acos(4πtₙ)
⇒ 4πtₙ=nπ±π/6⇒tₙ=n/4±1/24
Taking only the positive values for ‘t’,
t₁=1/24 s,t₂=5/24 s,t₃=7/24 s;t₄=11/24 s,t₅=13/24 s, etc.

[[img:6ed0310d5871]]
s: Let x₀ be the extension in the spring in equilibrium position and F₀ be the tension in the spring. Then F₀=kx₀ If T₀ is the tension in the string, then T₀=mf or 2T₀=F₀=kx₀ …(i) Let mass m be pulled downward through distance x, then tension in spring and string be F and T respectively. Now F=2T=k(x₀=x/2)=kx₀kx/2 or 2T=2T₀+kx/2 [from (i)] or T−T₀=kx/4 Restoring force on the mass m is f=T−mg=T−T₀=kx/4 …(ii) From (ii), f∝x and f is a restoring force, therefore, if mass m is left free, it will execute SHM. Here, spring factor =k/4, inertia factor =m. Time period, T=2π√(m/(k/4))=4π√(m/k)

t: A point particle of mass 0.1 kg is executing S.H.M. of amplitude 0.1 m. When the particle passes through the mean position, its kinetic energy is 8×10⁻³ joule. Obtain the equation of motion of this particle, if the initial phase of oscillation is 45°.
s:
The displacement of a particle in S.H.M. is given by y=asin(ωt+ϕ)
velocity =dy/dt=ωacos(ωt+ϕ)
The velocity is maximum when the particle passes through the mean position i.e.,
(dy/dt)ₘₐₓ=ω
The kinetic energy at this instant is given by
1/2 m(dy/dt)ₘₐₓ²=1/2 mω²a²=8×10⁻³ joule
or 1/2×(0.1)ω²×(0.1)²=8×10⁻³
Solving we get  ω=±4 Substituting the values of a,ω and ϕ in the equation of
S.H.M., we get y=0.1sin(±4t+π/4) metre

t: The amplitude of a damped oscillator becomes (1/3)ʳᵈ in 2 seconds. If its amplitude after 6 seconds is 1/n times the original amplitude, the value of n is
s:
Amplitude of a damped oscillator at any instant t is given by A=A₀e^(−bt/2 m)
where A₀ is the original amplitude From question, When t=2 s, A=A₀/3
∴A₀/3=A₀e^(−2 b/2 m)
or, 1/3=e^(−b/m)
When t=6 s, A=A₀/n
∴A₀/n=A₀e^(−6 b/2 m)
or, 1/n=e^(−3 b/m)=(e^(−b/m))³
or, 1/n=(1/3)³  (Using eq. (i))
∴n=3³=27

t: A particle executing SHM has velocities u and v, and magnitudes of acceleration a and b in two of its positions on the same side of the mean position. Find the distance between these two positions.
s:
In SHM: v²=ω²(A²−x²) and a_(eq)=ω²x
At position x₁: velocity =u, acceleration magnitude =a=ω²x₁
At position x₂: velocity =v, acceleration magnitude =b=ω²x₂
Subtracting velocity equations:
u²−v²=ω²(A²−x₁²)−ω²(A²−x₂²)=ω²(x₂²−x₁²)
u²−v²=(x₂−x₁)(ω²x₂+ω²x₁)=(x₂−x₁)(b+a)
Since both points are on the same side, d=x₂−x₁:
u²−v²=d(a+b)⇒d=(u²−v²)/(a+b)
Correct option: (1)

t: The time period of oscillations of a block attached to a spring is t₁. When the spring is replaced by another spring, the time period of the block is t₂. If both the springs are connected in series and the block is made to oscillate using the combination, then the time period of the block is

t:
Two identical springs are connected in series and parallel as shown in the figure. If fₛ and fₚ are frequencies of arrangements, what is fₛ/fₚ?
[[img:f6ecfd1aa59e]]
s:
In first case, springs are connected in parallel, so their equivalent spring constant
kₚ=k₁+k₂
So, frequency of this spring-block system is
fₚ=1/2π √(kₚ/m)
or fₚ=1/2π √((k₁+k₂)/m)
but k₁=k₂=k
∴ fₚ=1/2π √(2k/m) ..(i)
Now in second case, springs are connected in series, so their equivalent spring constant
k=k₁k₂/(k₁+k₂)
Hence, frequency of this arrangement is given by
fₛ=1/2π √(k₁k₂/((k₁+k₂)m))
or fₛ=1/2π √(k/2m) …(ii)
Dividing Eq. (ii) by Eq. (i), we get
fₛ/fₚ=(1/2π √(k/2m))/(1/2π √(2k/m))=√(1/4)
or fₛ/fₚ=1/2

t: A simple pendulum of length 40 cm oscillates with an angular amplitude of 0.04 rad. The time period is 2π/ω=2π/5s⁻¹=1.26 s
Linear amplitude =40 cm×0.04=1.6 cm

θ̇=(5 s⁻¹)√((0.04)²−(0.02)²)rad=0.17rad/s
where speed of the bob at this instant
V=θ̇A=(40 cm)×(0.17 s)=6.8 cm/s
At momentary rest, the bob is in extreme position. Thus, the angular acceleration |α|=ω²θ.
|α|=(0.04rad)(25 s⁻²)=1rad/s²

t₂=2x/v=(2×0.5)/1=1 second
This whole process is repeated. The block undergoes periodic motion with time period
T=t₁+t₂=(π/2+1) second

t: A hollow sphere is filled with water. It is hung by a long thread to make it a simple pendulum. As the water flows out of a hole at the bottom of the sphere, the frequency of oscillation will

Frequency of a simple pendulum

t: A simple pendulum of length l and a mass m of the bob is suspended in a car that is travelling with a constant speed v around a circle of radius R. If the pendulum undergoes small oscillations about its equilibrium position, the frequency of its oscillation will be

t: A particle of mass 0.50 kg executes a simple harmonic motion under a force F=−(50 N/m)x. If it crosses the centre of oscillation with a speed of 10 m/s, find the amplitude of motion.
s:
The kinetic energy of the particle when it is mean position, it is also its total energy as the potential energy is zero here.
E=1/2mv²=1/2(0.50 kg)(10 m/s)²=25 J
At the maximum displacement x=A, the speed is zero and hence the kinetic energy is zero. The potential energy here is 1/2kA². At this position it will also its total energy. Hence
1/2kA²=25 J ..(i)
The force on the particle is given by, F=−(50 N/m)x Thus, the spring constant is k=50 N/m.
Equation (i) gives
1/2(50 N/m)A²=25 J⇒A=1 m

t:
A uniform disc of mass m and radius R is pivoted smoothly at its centre of mass. A light spring of stiffness k is attached with the disc tangentially as shown in the Fig. Find the angular frequency in rad/s of torsional oscillations of the disc. (Take m=5 kg and K=10 N/m.)
[[img:1e8d515f4096]]
s:
If we twist (rotate) the disc through a small clockwise angle θ, the spring will be deformed (compressed) by a distance x=Rθ. Hence, the spring force Fₛ=kx=k(Rθ) will produce a restoring torque.
[[img:c5b5847d7a67]]
Restoring torque: τ=−F_SR where F_S=kRθ
This gives τ=−kR²θ
It means after removing the external (applied) torque, the restoring torque rotates the disc with an angular acceleration α which will bring the spring-disc system back to its original state.
Newton’s law of rotation (or torque equation): Applying Newton’s second law of rotation, we have
τ=I_Cα
where  τ=−kR²θ
This gives  α=−kR²θ/I_C  where  I_C=mR²/2
Then  a=−2k/mθ
Comparing the above equation with α=−ω²θ, we have
ω=√(2k/m)
After substituting the values we get ω=2rad/s.
